At VantaCon last week, a conversation about hiring pointed to a question more candidates are hearing in interviews: "How do you use AI?"

Imagine you have to compare quotes from several vendors. Each offered services and supplies, each with its own brands, sizes, and materials. Open your AI tool of preference, start speech-to-text, and brain-dump everything in your head; this is important. Writing an idea and talking about it are two different things.

"Here's what we have, here's what we need, here's what I think." About an hour later you will have data normalized, consumption forecasted, contract reviewed, and the raw data organized in case anyone needs to check your work.

Years ago, in Buenos Aires, I did a similar analysis by hand, copying and pasting years of logged hours to find out why a project kept losing money. It took me far longer. It also taught me what to look for.

A few weeks ago I wrote that AI might take away the practice that builds judgment. The hiring conversation was the other side of it: using AI well is its own practice, and if you haven't started, you're already behind.

For anyone in GRC, it's even more direct. As another panel put it: to govern AI, you have to use AI.

Both are true. So a good answer to "how do you use AI?" has three parts: → for work that's tedious but checkable, so judgment goes where it matters → with clear rules about which tools and which data, → and a plan for the time it gives back

So, how do you use AI?

❗️ Interesting development at LinkedIn ❗️

For the past 15 years, I've been using LinkedIn's Recruiter Professional Services (RPS) suite.
Over the years, prices have steadily increased. Fair enough, everything gets more expensive. That's business.

Recently, I reached out to renew several RPS licences. Nothing unusual, just another 12-month renewal, as we've done for years.

Until I received the following response:
"Unfortunately, we can no longer offer a 12-month renewal. As previously communicated, the standard contract term is now 36 months. As an exception, we could request a 24-month agreement. The annual price would be €10,760 per licence per year"

A price increase of approximately 70%.

The reasoning?
It's still RPS, just now called RPS+. The '+' apparently stands for additional Sales Navigator functionality and LinkedIn's new AI-powered Hiring Assistant.

Really don't need it. 

Especially when you consider the growing number of alternative platforms entering the recruitment technology space. Think Metaview, Hunter, FullEnreach, Lusha and others.

So, fellow recruiters; Any thoughts on this?

AI in RevOps has moved from slideware to real workflows.

That was my biggest takeaway from the CRO Exchange Miami floor. I spent time with several AI teams, and I left more optimistic than I arrived.

Having built RevOps from startup to scale-up to global enterprise, this is what I look for in AI offerings:

1⃣ Pay on results, not delivery. Share the upside, and share the risk.
2⃣ Short contracts. Confident products earn their renewal.
3⃣ Try before you buy. A 30–60 day pilot on real data, with success criteria agreed upfront.
4⃣ Shared KPIs. Agree the baseline together, then measure against it.
5⃣ Trust by design. Enterprise-grade security, no training on customer data, and explainable outputs.
6⃣ Live in weeks, not quarters. Native to the CRM, and in the reps' flow of work.

Where AI can make the biggest difference, and what good looks like:

🎯 Lead gen: pipeline, not activity.
→ A clear lift in meeting-to-stage-2 conversion, not just more meetings booked
→ Speed-to-lead in minutes, not hours
→ Cost per qualified opportunity that falls quarter on quarter

📊 Sales Ops: predictability is the product.
→ Forecast within ±5% of the final number by week 6 of the quarter
→ The "why" behind every at-risk deal, not just a score
→ Comp scenarios modelled in days, not weeks, with fewer disputes after payout

🔁 Post-sales: retention is where AI pays for itself.
→ Churn risk flagged 90+ days before renewal
→ Whitespace mapped across every key account
→ A measurable lift in NRR within two renewal cycles

In my experience, the hardest problems were never a lack of data. They were a lack of time to act on it. That's the gap these teams are setting out to close.

What stood out from my conversations:

🔹 Zig.ai (Steve Ancheta): AI agents across research, prospecting and outreach, with billing tied to verified work completed. A bold move towards outcome-based pricing.
🔹 Othello (Jared Zelman): real-time coaching while the buyer is still on the line.
🔹 Hyperbound (Sriharsha Guduguntla): AI roleplay plus real-call scoring, from hiring to onboarding to coaching.
🔹 Yoodli (Varun Puri): AI roleplays that let reps rehearse a conversation before the real buyer.
🔹 SiftHub (Colin Casad): AI for RFPs and security questionnaires, aimed at faster presales and shorter cycles.

Thank you all for the conversations. 

The tools are ready. The real question is whether our operating models are ready for them.

A special thank you to Vincent Rama, Yukta Venugopal, Erick Coronel at CRO Exchange for a brilliantly run event that brought senior sales and revenue leaders and AI innovators into the same room.

Someone asked me yesterday what certification they should get to break into AI. I told them none.  Not because credentials are worthless. Because the hiring managers I know stopped reading them.  What actually moves the needle right now:  1. Evidence you can ship. A messy project that runs beats a perfect certificate. 2. Depth in one weird corner. Eval pipelines, data contracts, RL environments. Boring and specific wins. 3. The ability to explain your thinking. Interviews are filtering for judgment now, not trivia.  The copilot era flattened the base layer of the skill stack. Anyone can generate decent code or decent strategy text. What's scarce is someone who can tell when the output is wrong.  Which would you bet on: shipping, depth, or judgment?  #AI #Careers #CareerAdvice #GenAI #JobSearch

Welcome Andrew Smith, Founder and CEO at Swapt on this episode of 🔥 The Lantern 🔥

If you sell on Amazon, you don't get access to your customer's email. Swapt fixes that!

The team identifies customers across marketplaces, captures the email, and runs them through retention marketing flows to get repurchases quickly.

🔍 What are Andrew and his team building at Swapt? 🔎

Swapt has become a multifaceted business. Its roots began in digital marketing, and now it reaches into supply chains, which is one of the company's big differentiators. 

A lot of companies pitch the last mile, getting that next purchase. Swapt focuses on making every step in between easy.

📈 What drove Swapt’s growth in 2026? 📈

Going after the very hardest problems. How do you get the QR codes onto the packaging? Are you going through the contract manufacturer or the warehouse? Who are your suppliers? 

That took Swapt from zero to seven figures of revenue and landing logos like Grüns and AG1. 

Swapt built connections in Hong Kong and across the United States so brands can get their products ready for Swapt fast. That was the unlock.

🤔 What learnings would Andrew pass back to other Founders? 🤔

Focus on your problem, a lot. 

AI has made development far easier, but Andrew considers it a methodology, not the business. 

Defensibility comes from how deeply ingrained you are in solving the problem easily for your customers. Focus too much on the methodology...and you miss what drives revenue!

🤝 How can we help Swapt? 🤝

Talent. Some of Swapt's biggest unlocks have come from hiring someone who gets it. 

The team is methodical, bringing on one person at a time, sometimes as the only new hire for three months, to make sure the fit is right. If you join, you’ll get a $7 coffee on the company every week and promotion cycles every six months. Check out the Swapt team!

I attended the HSE summit recently organized by Julia Nimchinski (I highly recommend you to attend to her summits. The discussions are genuinely interesting) and forward-deployed engineers was one of the main topics. 

One panel predicted that FDEs will constantly change its form, mainly because of AI evolution, and that a maintenance gap opens when a FDE leaves a project. FDEs exist because of agentic AI. The workflows are non-deterministic and custom-built, so someone has to embed deep in the business and co-create the system instead of installing existing software. The IP stays with you but that is just 1 part of the outcome. 

The other part: the Engineers who built it may or may not stay with you, let's be honest, no vendor can guarantee that you will keep an Engineer forever, I've seen looooong engagements, but none forever, and at the current AI hiring pace, anyone who promises that is selling you something + its not always about attrition or retention, your own company's strategic shifts can make you let go your beloved contractor.

Tooba Durraze, Ph.D. put it in a nutshell: the disillusionment comes "when FDEs step out and a whole year has gone by".

You should have a very important conversation before you sign that contract, and it's not about how fast the engineers embed. It's about what happens to the system if the FDE leaves, and who maintains it.

It’s better to have a quick answer now than find out in month 14.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗦𝘆𝗻𝘁𝗮𝘅 𝗜𝘀 𝗙𝗿𝗲𝗲, 𝗔𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗜𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗢𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗠𝗼𝗮𝘁

For twenty years, software economics were dictated by a single bottleneck: writing code was slow, expensive, and scarce. Everything—from how we staffed teams to how we scoped product roadmaps—was built around the cost of production.

AI has inverted that math. Syntax generation is now effectively deflationary.

Just last month, putting on my federal enterprise architect hat, I generated a complex, end-to-end system specification in forty-eight hours—work that historically took a cross-functional team weeks of whiteboarding and documentation cycles.

Yet in complex, interconnected environments, generating artifacts and code faster doesn't automatically mean shipping resilient software faster. In fact, unchecked velocity creates a dangerous new trap: 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗼𝗻𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, 𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘂𝗿𝗲.

If every competitor has access to the same foundational models, differentiation no longer comes from how fast you generate the middle.Economic value migrates violently to two critical bookends of the product lifecycle:

1. 𝗙𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗕𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗘𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 LLMs are ruthless amplifiers. Generating a complex spec over a weekend only works when you bring deep domain constraints to the table first. If your product requirements and regulatory rules are ambiguous, AI will simply manufacture architectural debt at ten times the speed. The scarcest talent in the room isn't the developer prompting a model—it is the systems architect who can translate messy operational reality into crisp, machine-verifiable specifications before a single line of code is generated.

2. 𝗛𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗥𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝗕𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗿𝘆 Getting a prototype to pass a demo is trivial; guaranteeing deterministic behavior across a federated system-of-systems is not. Real platform value lives in automated verification—enforcing strict data contracts, zero-trust isolation, and continuous compliance gates that contain the blast radius when synthetic code meets production load.

The organizations that win this next cycle won't be the ones generating the most code. They will be the ones building 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻-𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁, 𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻-𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝘀—and hiring the product leaders who know how to govern systemic complexity at scale.

Hiring is tragic these days.

I recently hired two professionals: one for end-to-end website development, and one as a senior content writer for web copy, blogs, and white papers. 

It's an AI-positioning revamp, and I was handling the project myself.

During the interviews, I was promised a lot. I checked everything. I interviewed thoroughly. Everything looked good.

What went wrong was communication.

Even with a signed contract and a timeline in place, the effort just isn't there. 

The work is being taken lightly. I calculated everything from my end. 

This was barely a one-month project. It's now been over a month, then over another month, and it's still not final.

When I confront them, I get one answer: "There were festivals."

Yes, I know there were. But I asked every question upfront. Can you do this? Can you deliver in this time? And the answer was yes.

I know, Ai exists, I get it. 

But if you've been a content writer for 5 to 6 years, you should know how to put your own brain into a piece.

I genuinely don't know where the professional economy is heading, or where the actual effort has gone. 

But I'm sure it isn't anywhere good, professional, or productive.

All it leads to is money burned, time lost, energy drained, and irritation. 

Add the stress, and you know what science says about that.

Have you faced this too? I'd like to know how you're handling it.

Industry spotlight: SaaS / AI 🚀

Had a great conversation this week with the CEO of a profitable AI company that’s raising a seed round and looking at non-dilutive funding alongside it.

They have the cash to do it themselves. So why look at funding?

1️⃣ Headroom, not necessity. They’re cash-flow positive, but want an extra buffer so they never have to choose between growth and a safe runway.
2️⃣ Hiring ahead of revenue. A major contract starts in Q1, and they need 2-3 hires in place before the first invoice goes out.
3️⃣ Payment timing. Even with 30-day terms, a new customer’s first payment can land 45-60 days after invoicing. Funding bridges that gap.
4️⃣ Equity timing. Seed rounds can take longer to close than expected. Non-dilutive funding means hiring doesn’t have to wait on the round.

The takeaway: the strongest businesses often use funding as a strategic choice rather than a last resort. Keep your cash for the unexpected, and let funding cover the predictable.

If you’re a SaaS or AI founder planning hires or a big contract ahead of a raise, I’d be happy to chat. 🤝

There's a new PM title showing up in job postings: Forward Deployed Product Manager. Scale AI, BetterUp, and Accenture are just a few hiring for it. I read their job description to see what the role actually does.

Dr. Nancy Li called it "the new hot Product role" where a traditional PM asks, "What should we build?”. An FDPM asks, "How do we make this actually work for the customer and expand the account's value?"

Here's what one of the postings says about the job:

1. You own product outcomes for the highest-impact enterprise accounts. You're the PM accountable for delivery and the value the customer gets.
2. You take deployments from a signed contract into production. 
3. You turn real customer workflows, friction, and priorities into product input for the core platform teams. That input is specific, backed by evidence, and clear about tradeoffs.
4. You partner closely with forward deployed engineers (FDEs), so the account runs as one coordinated team.
5. You find room to expand the account, based on value the customer has already seen.

My read is that this is really a role for an experienced PM who owns delivery for one specific customer profile. You’re still on the hook for product outcomes, just for the highest-impact enterprise accounts. Your team works more like customer-facing engineers who get a working solution deployed, and the PM decides what to improve once it’s live. Along the way, you might also scope features that end up helping the broader platform and every type of customer. You’ll leverage data to improve and fine-tune what the customer will experience. 

I recommend PMs to double down on the soft skills they’ve built and start to apply a systems thinking mindset when asking to turn real workflows into production-level experiences. You’ll be able to transition to this type of role as more companies adopt LLMs/non-deterministic products to their offerings.
